answer.answer:
**Summary**

A robot builds when four things are in place at once: a machine to act with, sensing that tells it where it is, work standardised and prefabricated enough to be picked and placed, and a trained workforce with a management system wrapped around the whole chain. The largest single requirement is not hardware: workforce training is drawn on by 44 of the 50 coded cases, against 22 for the robotic arm and 39 for scanning and sensing, so the binding constraint is organisational as much as technical. Path-planning cannot run without on-board sensing and point-cloud geometry, and it is itself constrained by site conditions, which is why most deployed work sits in standardised, repetitive packages. One route often assumed to make on-site robotic assembly possible, a mobile factory enclosing the work, is asserted in the literature and carried by none of the 50 cases.

**Detailed answer**

*The machine and the act of assembly*

The core act, PR4 "Robotic assembly" (Process), is drawn on by 13 of the 50 coded cases [1]. Its stated requirement is the machine itself: PR4 dependsOn RE2 "Robotic arm", robotic assembly requires a robot arm, an edge carried by 12 of the 50 cases and backed by peer-reviewed evidence [1], with the same relation asserted in the enabling direction, RE2 enablesCapability PR4, carried by 12 of the 50 [1]. RE2 is drawn on by 22 of the 50 cases [1]. A second machine route exists for printing rather than placing: PR3 "Additive manufacturing" dependsOn RE3 "3D printer", carried by 3 of the 50 [1], and PR3 itself is drawn on by only 4 of the 50 cases [1], against 5 for RE10 "Gantry-type robotic system", which carries no dependency edges at all [1].

*What the work has to look like before a robot can do it*

Two upstream conditions on the work package, neither of them a machine: AT7 "Highly standardised" (Attribute) enablesCapability PR4, on the finding that Japanese automated erection systems rely on standardised prefabricated components, carried by 10 of the 50 cases [1], and PR4 hasPrecondition PR2 "Prefabrication/off-site", automated overhead delivery and assembly requiring extensive prefabrication and unification of materials, carried by 4 of the 50 [1]. AT7 is drawn on by 25 of the 50 cases [1] and PR2 by 20 of the 50 [1]. There is also an organisational precondition that is easy to miss: PR4 dependsOn RI12 "Delivery/business model/work culture", robotics adoption in precast production resting on the environmental and organisational context, carried by only 2 of the 50 [1].

The commonly cited route to relaxing these constraints on site is CO12 "Mobile factory", a Condition and not a machine. CO12 enablesCapability PR4 on the argument that an enclosure lets welding and assembly proceed in a normal manner even in rain, and that edge is carried by 0 of the 50 coded cases [1]; CO12 amplifies VA2 "Reduce time/improve productivity/efficiency" is likewise carried by 0 of the 50 [1]. CO12 is drawn on by 1 of the 50 cases [1], and PR8 "On-site DFAB" hasPrecondition CO12 is carried by 1 [1]. Cited in the literature, exhibited by essentially none of the record.

*Knowing where to move: sensing and path-planning*

PR12 "Path-planning" is drawn on by 26 of the 50 cases [1] and enablesCapability PR4, path planning being a precondition for robotic assembly, though that edge is carried by only 2 of the 50 [1]. Its own requirements are the strongest sensing claim in this material: PR12 hasPrecondition RE4 "3D scanner/sensor/camera/ICT", localisation via onboard sensors being a fundamental prerequisite for autonomous operation, carried by 22 of the 50 [1], and PR12 dependsOn CO16 "3D point-cloud", carried by 9 of the 50 [1]. RE4 is drawn on by 39 of the 50 cases [1]. Software feeds the same node: RE1 "Parametric/computational/data-driven algorithm/machine code" enablesCapability PR12, carried by 7 of the 50 [1] and RE8 "Machine Learning/AI algorithm" enablesCapability PR12, carried by 5 [1]. And the site pushes back: RI5 "Location dependent/site constraint" constrains PR12, since reliable GNSS signals are typically unavailable indoors, carried by 15 of the 50 [1].

*The workflow and the people around it*

AR9 "Automated production workflow" is drawn on by 44 of the 50 coded cases [1], the nearest thing here to "a robot building" as a whole. It is fed by RE9 "Project management system", whose enablesCapability edge to AR9 is carried by 26 of the 50 [1], by CO3 "BIM-based environment", carried by 8 [1], and by RE13 "IFC", carried by 1 [1]. Its one stated requirement is human: AR9 dependsOn RI6 "Require workforce training", on the finding that the sophistication of digital technologies prohibits adoption by less technologically familiar workers, carried by 38 of the 50 [1], and RI6 is drawn on by 44 of the 50 cases [1]. The same requirement sits under collaborative work: CO6 "Human-robot interaction" dependsOn RI6, carried by 27 of the 50 [1]. What follows downstream is AR9 enablesCapability VA1 "Reduce human dependency", carried by 42 of the 50 [1].

Safety and regulation appear as dependencies rather than as afterthoughts: AT3 "Bespoke DFAB technology" dependsOn RI18 "Regulatory/legal concern", robot technology design and integration depending on baseline safety-standard compliance, standard-grade evidence, carried by 9 of the 50 [1], and CO6 mitigates RI20 "Work safety concern" through power-and-force-limiting collaborative operation, carried by 4 of the 50 [1].

*The deployed record*

Four deployed processes here show what this looks like in service, all at technology readiness level 9. census_RXH1-1 performs assembly, steelwork and welding on the structural core and the building envelope, facade or curtain wall, adopted to address integration [2], manufactured by Firm_013. census_RXH4-1 performs assembly and concrete work on the structural core and envelope, adopted to address cost and labor [3], from Firm_166. census_RXH7-2 performs assembly and tiling on the building envelope, facade or curtain wall, adopted to address quality, safety, labor and market [4], manufactured by Firm_125 and a record of process RP29. census_RXH3-4 performs inspection and material handling on the envelope, adopted to address digital, quality and labor [5], developed by Firm_144 and a record of RP8. The context does not link any of these four to particular enablers, so I cannot say which of the requirements above each one exhibits; what they do establish is that the deployed work sits in envelope and structural packages of exactly the standardised, repetitive kind that AT7 and PR2 describe.

*Two cautions on reading this*

The retrieval widened "build" to cover the design-side enablers as well, which adds one finding worth flagging: AT4 "Automated design optimisation/generative design" is drawn on by 1 of the 50 cases [1], and the edge from RE8 "Machine Learning/AI algorithm" to it is carried by 0 of the 50 [1]. Generative design is not, on this record, part of what makes a robot build. Second, the edges listed above are complete for the enablers reached by this question and their counts may be quoted as totals, but the co-occurrence list is a cut of the strongest 15 out of 2318 co-occurrence edges touching these enablers [1] and is statistical, not a dependency claim, so nothing there should be read as a requirement.
